tools.name: observe
tools.description: Apply constant force in N for duration in s from rest at position zero. Each call resets the object. Returns position in m and velocity in m/s.

execution_limits.note: Program call limit includes cached and invalid calls; unique attempt limit is shared across rounds.

experiment.description: Executable Python source only. No prose, Markdown or code fences. Use call(name, dict) and emit(value); responses are dictionaries.

response.question: Does the object obey ideal Newtonian dynamics with constant mass and no drag, or does it show drag, a force threshold, or nonlinear force response?
response.experiment:
results = []
probes = [
    (1, 1),
    (2, 1),
    (1, 2),
    (0, 1),
    (-1, 1),
    (10, 1),
    (1, 0.5),
    (5, 2),
    (0.1, 1),
    (1, 5),
]
for force, duration in probes:
    resp = call("observe", {"force": force, "duration": duration})
    entry = {"force": force, "duration": duration, "status": resp.get("status")}
    if resp.get("status") == "ok":
        entry["result"] = resp.get("result")
        entry["evidence_id"] = resp.get("evidence_id")
    results.append(entry)
emit(results)

hypotheses.statement: Ideal Newtonian point mass with constant mass m and no drag: x = 0.5*(F/m)*t^2, v = (F/m)*t.
hypotheses.prediction: At fixed duration, x and v are exactly proportional to F; at fixed force, x is exactly proportional to t^2 and v to t; F=0 gives x=0 and v=0; F=-1 mirrors F=1 with opposite signs.
hypotheses.falsification: Any deviation from exact proportionality (e.g., x(2F) != 2*x(F), x(2t) != 4*x(t), nonzero motion at F=0, or asymmetry under sign reversal) refutes H1.

hypotheses.statement: Linear viscous drag with constant mass: m dv/dt = F - gamma*v, so velocity saturates and position grows sub-quadratically in time.
hypotheses.prediction: At fixed force, v(t) approaches a terminal value F/gamma and x(t) grows roughly linearly at large t; at fixed duration, x and v remain proportional to F if m and gamma are constant.
hypotheses.falsification: If v grows linearly without saturation over the tested durations, or if x(t) matches t^2 exactly, H2 is disfavored.

hypotheses.statement: Nonlinear or threshold response: either a static friction threshold (small forces produce no motion) or a force-dependent effective mass (x not proportional to F).
hypotheses.prediction: A small force such as F=0.1 may yield zero or disproportionately small displacement; x(2F) may not equal 2*x(F); or a force threshold appears.
hypotheses.falsification: If F=0.1 produces motion consistent with the same proportionality seen at larger forces, and x scales linearly with F, H3 is disfavored.

experiment.description: Executable Python source only. No prose, Markdown or code fences. Use call(name, dict) and emit(value); responses are dictionaries.

interpretations.claim: Observed regularity: at fixed duration, position and velocity scale linearly with force: E2 is about 2x E1, E6 about 10x E1, E9 about 0.1x E1 at t=1 s; E8 is about 5x E3 at t=2 s; E5 is about -E1; E4 is zero. This is consistent with no static threshold and a linear force response in the tested range.
interpretations.scope: F in [-1, 10] N plus 0.1 N, mainly t=1 s; one t=2 s force check; single object, reset each call.
uncertainties: No test below 0.1 N or above 10 N.
No test of negative forces other than -1 N.
Force scaling at durations other than 1 s and 2 s is only partially checked.

interpretations.claim: Observed regularity: at F=1 N, motion is sub-quadratic in time: x(2)/x(1) is about 3.80 versus 4, and x(5)/x(1) is about 20.47 versus 25; velocity is sublinear: v(2)/v(1) is about 1.85 versus 2, and v(5)/v(1) is about 3.71 versus 5. This disfavors ideal Newtonian motion with no drag over the tested durations.
uncertainties: Time scaling was measured mainly at one force.
Finite precision and unknown measurement noise may affect small deviations.

interpretations.claim: Leading explanation: linear viscous drag with constant mass, m dv/dt = F - gamma v, fits the data. A rough fit from E1 and E3 gives gamma/m about 0.16 s^-1, m about 3.77 kg, and gamma about 0.60 kg/s, and predicts E10 within about 0.5%.
interpretations.scope: F=1-5 N, t=0.5-5 s, assuming constant m and gamma and no other forces.
uncertainties: Parameters are approximate and not uniquely identified from finite data.
Other velocity-dependent or time-dependent models may also fit.
No independent mass or drag measurement is available.

interpretations.claim: Observed regularity: short-duration E7 is consistent with drag: v(0.5)/v(1) is about 0.520, above 0.5, and x(0.5)/x(1) is about 0.257, above 0.25, as expected for velocity-dependent drag rather than constant acceleration.
interpretations.scope: F=1 N, t=0.5 s versus 1 s.
uncertainties: Small deviations could be affected by timing or measurement precision.
Only one short-duration point is available.

remaining_unknowns: Whether velocity approaches a finite terminal value F/gamma at long durations, as linear viscous drag predicts.
Whether the drag law remains linear at higher speeds or forces beyond the tested range.
Whether mass and drag coefficient are constant across all forces and durations.
Whether a threshold exists below 0.1 N.
Whether behavior is symmetric for negative forces other than -1 N.
Exact parameter values and measurement noise level.
review.suggested_next_question: Does the velocity approach a finite terminal value F/gamma at long durations, as linear viscous drag predicts, or continue to grow without saturation?
